questions.question: _________ are known as narrow money.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **M1 and M2**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points:__**Money - 

 
• In a modern economy, money consists mainly of currency notes and coins issued by the monetary authority of the country.
 
• In India currency notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which is the monetary authority in India.
 
• However, coins are issued by the Government of India.
 
• Apart from currency notes and coins, the balance in savings, or current account deposits, held by the public in commercial banks is also considered money since cheques drawn on these accounts are used to settle transactions.
 
• Such deposits are called demand deposits as they are payable by the bank on demand from the account holder.
 
• Other deposits, e.g. fixed deposits, have a fixed period to maturity and are referred to as time deposits. 

Money supply - 

 
• The total stock of money in circulation among the public at a particular point in time is called money supply. 
 
• RBI publishes figures for four alternative measures of money supply, viz. M1, M2, M3, and M4.
 
• They are defined as follows -
 
 
• M1 = Currency + Demand deposits with the banking system. 
 
• M2 = M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks
 
• M3 = M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks
 
• M4 = M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organizations (excluding National Savings Certificates)
 
 
 
• M1 and M2 are narrow money. 
 
• M3 and M4 are known as broad money.
 
• These gradations are in decreasing order of liquidity. M1 is the most liquid and easiest for transactions whereas M4 is the least liquid of all. M3 is the most commonly used measure of the money supply.
 
• It is also known as aggregate monetary resources.

questions.question: Which regulatory body in India is responsible for overseeing and regulating Micro Finance Institutions?

questions.question: RBI defined M1 as CU + DD. What is DD?

options.text: Net demand deposits held by International banks only
Net demand deposits held by RBI
Net demand deposits held by SBI
Net demand deposits held by commercial banks

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 4**__**. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the context of the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI) defining M1, "DD" stands for Demand Deposits.**
 
• **Demand Deposits** represent the net demand deposits held by commercial banks.
 
• **Demand Deposits** are a type of bank account from which deposited funds can be withdrawn at any time without any notice to the bank.
 
• These types of accounts include checking accounts, savings accounts, or any other type of bank account that allows for the immediate withdrawal of funds.
 
• They are considered to be highly liquid assets and are included in the calculation of the** M1 money supply.**
 
• **Net Demand Deposits** would account for the total of these deposits held by a bank, minus any amounts that the bank has itself deposited with other banks.
 
• This gives a more accurate view of a bank's liquidity and the amount of money readily available in the economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Currency **(notes and coins in circulation with the public and vault cash of banks) **- denoted as **CU.**
 
• **Demand Deposits of the public (DD) **with commercial banks.

questions.question: For which of the following sources of financial resources may financial intermediation NOT be required?

__
 
• **Family funds** are financial resources that can be obtained directly from family members without the need for financial intermediation.

• Direct financing, such as using family funds, bypasses these intermediaries and can be a quicker way to secure necessary funds.
 
• However, relying solely on family funds may limit the amount of capital available compared to institutional sources.

questions.question: A type of loan that allows borrowers to make low payments in the initial phases but repayment of the balance amount in lump sum at maturity is known as _______.
questions.solution:
Correct Answer **Balloon Mortgage**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** In this type of loan,** borrowers make low payments** for a **certain period of time** and then **pay off the remaining balance** in **one large lump sum, or "balloon" payment**, at the **end of the loan term.**

**Initial Low Payments:**

 
• Balloon loans typically have lower initial payments compared to traditional loans.
 
• This is because these payments are primarily based on the interest of the loan, not the principal.

**Lump Sum Payment:**

 
• The defining feature of a balloon loan is the large "balloon" payment due at the end of the loan term.
 
• This payment covers the remaining principal of the loan.

**Short Term: **

 
• Balloon loans usually have shorter terms than traditional installment loans.
 
• The term is often 5 to 7 years, but the balloon payment is based on what the balance would be after a longer term, often 30 years.

**Risk of Default:**

 
• There is a higher risk of default with balloon loans.
 
• If borrowers cannot make the large balloon payment at the end of the term, they may need to refinance the loan, sell the asset, or default on the loan.

**Common in Real Estate:**

 
• Balloon loans are often used in real estate transactions, particularly for commercial properties or short-term real estate investments.
 
• They can also be used for personal loans and auto loans.

questions.question:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Prof. Walker** is credited with the statement "Money is what money does."
 
• The statement emphasizes the functional definition of money, focusing on its role and activities in the economy rather than its intrinsic properties.
 
• Money serves several key functions: a medium of exchange, a unit of account, a store of value, and sometimes, a standard of deferred payment.
 
• This perspective aligns with the pragmatic approach in economics, where the utility and effectiveness of money are determined by its practical applications.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prof. Walker** was an influential economist whose work significantly impacted monetary theory.
 
• The pragmatic view of money has been pivotal in understanding its evolving forms, from physical currency to digital money.
 
• This definition underscores the adaptability of money to different economic contexts and technological advancements.
 
• Understanding the functions of money helps in grasping the broader economic principles and the impact of monetary policy.

questions.question: What does the term ‘Overdraft’ mean in banking?

options.text: The process of transferring funds between bank accounts
The maximum withdrawal limit from an ATM

The correct answer is __**Short-term financing facility**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Short-term financing facility** is what the term 'Overdraft' means in banking.
 
• An overdraft allows an account holder to withdraw more money than what is available in their bank account.
 
• It is a type of short-term loan provided by banks to help cover temporary cash shortfalls.
 
• The bank charges interest on the overdrawn amount, and there may also be fees associated with the overdraft facility.
 
• Overdrafts are useful for managing cash flow and unexpected expenses, ensuring that transactions are not declined due to insufficient funds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The interest rate on an overdraft can be higher compared to other types of loans.
 
• Overdraft limits are typically set by the bank based on the customer's creditworthiness and account history.
 
• Exceeding the overdraft limit can result in additional penalties and higher interest rates.
 
• It is important for account holders to monitor their account balances regularly to avoid excessive overdraft fees.
 
• Some banks offer overdraft protection services, which link the primary account to another account or line of credit to cover overdrafts.

questions.question:
While estimating Gross Domestic Product, the monetary value of only final goods are considered because ________.

a. its immobility, the active economic flow is ended.

b. of the issues of double counting

c. the value added at each stage of the production process is included
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Only b**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the economic performance of a country by calculating the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given time period.
 
• Only the value of final goods is considered to avoid the issue of double counting, which occurs if intermediate goods are counted multiple times in the production process.
 
• Double counting can lead to an inflated and inaccurate measure of the GDP, as it would count the same value more than once.
 
• Intermediate goods are not included in GDP calculations since their value is already encapsulated in the price of the final goods.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**

 
 
• GDP is the total monetary or market value of all the finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
 
• It serves as a comprehensive scorecard of a country’s economic health.
 
• GDP can be measured using three approaches: production (or output or value added) approach, income approach, and expenditure approach.
 
 
 
• **Final Goods**
 
 
• Final goods are goods that have been completed and are ready for sale to the end consumer.
 
• Examples include cars, household appliances, and groceries.
 
 
 
• **Intermediate Goods**
 
 
• Intermediate goods are products used in the production of final goods or services.
 
• Examples include raw materials like steel, wood, and other components that are used in manufacturing.
 
 
 
• **Value Added**
 
 
• Value added refers to the additional value created at each stage of production.
 
• It is the difference between the cost of inputs and the value of outputs.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is true?

A) Wage bill of the government is a capital expenditure.

B) Disinvestment by the government in a company is a capital receipt.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is__** Option 4**__. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Disinvestment by the government in a company can be either a capital receipt or a revenue receipt, depending on the nature of the transaction.**
 
• If the government sells its equity shares in a company to the public or to another entity, the proceeds from the sale are considered a capital receipt.
 
• This is because the government is selling a **capital asset **(i.e., its ownership stake in the company) and receiving cash in return.
 
• However, if the government sells its goods or services to a company, such as land or buildings, the proceeds from the sale would be considered a revenue receipt.
 
• This is because the government is receiving cash for the sale of goods or services, which is a normal business transaction and not the sale of a capital asset.
 
• In summary, **the classification of disinvestment receipts as capital or revenue depends on the nature of the transaction and the asset being sold.**

**​** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• In accounting and finance, capital expenditures refer to investments made by a company or government that are expected to provide long-term benefits, such as the acquisition of fixed assets like** land, buildings, equipment, and machinery.**
 
• These assets are expected to generate revenue or other economic benefits over a long period of time.
 
• On the other hand, the wage bill of the government is typically considered an operating expenditure because it represents the cost of the government's day-to-day operations.
 
• This includes the salaries and wages paid to government employees, which are necessary to keep the government functioning and to provide public services.
 
• While there may be instances where the government's wage bill is considered a capital expenditure, such as when it is tied to a specific capital project, such as the construction of a new building or infrastructure project, in general, it is considered an operating expenditure rather than a capital expenditure.

questions.question: As per ’Basel III: A global regulatory framework for more resilient banks and banking systems’ released in December 2010, banks will be required to hold a capital conservation buffer of ______ of risk weighted assets (RWAs) in the form of common equity to withstand future periods of stress.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2.5%.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Basel III** is a set of international banking regulations developed by the Bank for International Settlements in order to promote stability in the international financial system.
 
• The **Basel Committee** published the Basel III rules text in **December 2010.**
 
• It covers the worldwide regulatory criteria on bank capital adequacy and liquidity that were agreed upon by the Governors and Heads of Supervision and adopted by the** G20 Leaders** at their November summit in Seoul.
 
• To withstand future periods of stress, banks will be required to keep a capital conservation buffer of **2.5%**__ of risk-weighted assets (RWAs) in the form of common equity under Basel III.
 
• The results of the Committee's complete **quantitative impact research** were also released (QIS).
 
• **Nout Wellink** was the Chairman of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision.
 
• Basel Committee on Banking Supervision examines and proposes ways to reconfigure global banking regulations.
 
• The Committee estimated that Group 1 banks in aggregate would have had a shortfall of €577 billion at the end of 2009.
 
• The Basel III accord increased the minimum Basel III capital requirements for banks from 2% in Basel II to 4.5% of common equity, as a percentage of the bank’s risk-weighted assets.
 
• In order to be Basel compliant, there is additionally a 2.5% buffer capital requirement, bringing the total minimum requirement to 7%.
 
• When banks are in financial distress, they can use the buffer, but doing so can result in even more financial constraints when it comes to paying dividends.

• **Treasury bills** are short-term government securities issued at a discount but by the government, not commercial banks.

questions.question: ____ refers to the measure related to the sale of assets for the achievement of some purpose.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Liquidation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Liquidation is the process of bringing a business to an end and distributing its assets to claimants.
 
• It typically occurs when a company is insolvent, meaning it cannot pay its obligations as and when they come due.
 
• The assets of the company are sold off and the proceeds are used to pay off debts, liabilities, and expenses.
 
• Any remaining funds are distributed to the shareholders of the company.
 
• Liquidation can be voluntary or involuntary, depending on whether the decision is made by the shareholders or forced by creditors through court action.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Insolvency**

 
 
• Insolvency is a state where an individual or organization can no longer meet its financial obligations with its lender or lenders as debts become due.
 
• Insolvency can lead to bankruptcy if the insolvent entity is unable to come to an agreement with creditors to restructure debt.
 
• Insolvency is of two types: cash-flow insolvency and balance-sheet insolvency.
 
 
 
• **Bankruptcy**
 
 
• Bankruptcy is a legal proceeding involving a person or business that is unable to repay their outstanding debts.
 
• The bankruptcy process begins with a petition filed by the debtor or on behalf of creditors.
 
• All of the debtor's assets are measured and evaluated, and the assets may be used to repay a portion of outstanding debt.
 
 
 
• **Receivership**
 
 
• Receivership is a legal process in which a receiver is appointed by a court to manage the property, business, or assets of a financially distressed company.
 
• The receiver's role is to recover funds owed to creditors and distribute any remaining assets to stakeholders.
 
• Receivership is often seen as a last resort before liquidation.
 
 
 
• **Voluntary Liquidation**
 
 
• Voluntary liquidation occurs when the shareholders of a company decide to wind up its affairs and dissolve the company.
 
• This decision is often made when a company has fulfilled its purpose or when it is financially beneficial to dissolve the entity.
 
• The process involves selling off the company's assets, paying off creditors, and distributing any remaining funds to shareholders.
 
 
 
• **Involuntary Liquidation**
 
 
• Involuntary liquidation occurs when creditors force a company into liquidation through court action due to unpaid debts.
 
• This type of liquidation is often initiated when creditors believe they will not recover their funds through normal business operations.
 
• The court appoints a liquidator to sell off the company's assets and distribute the proceeds to creditors.
